blocks.body: Lab 07 showed line of sight, terrain, and a first skywave picture. This lab is the wave itself and the other paths a Technician is expected to recognize. Every picture is an educational model, not a forecast.
Raise an antenna and watch a classroom horizon. Then move a vehicle and watch the signal flutter before you learn the name.
Separate absorption from a returned wave. Sketch HF against VHF. Then match the special paths: sporadic E, meteor scatter, aurora, tropospheric ducting, and a ridge that still leaks a signal.

blocks.prompt: Why can two stations using the same power and frequency have very different results at different times or locations?
blocks.reference: Power and frequency do not choose the path by themselves. A ridge, a reflection, vegetation, rain, the time of day, a meteor, a patch of sporadic E, or a temperature inversion can open or close the route between the same two stations. The wave's electric and magnetic fields are still there. What changes is the medium and the geometry they travel through.

blocks.body: Radio Lab practice. These items use the models you just ran. They are not official exam questions.

questions.stem: In this lab's wave model, which field direction is the polarization?
questions.why: The electric and magnetic fields are perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel. Polarization follows the electric field.

questions.stem: A 14 MHz wave and a 146 MHz wave are both in free space. Which one travels faster in this lab?
choices: Neither. They share the same free-space speed
14 MHz, because the wavelength is longer
146 MHz, because the frequency is higher
questions.why: Free-space speed does not depend on frequency. The higher frequency has the shorter wavelength, about 300 divided by the frequency in megahertz.

questions.stem: Which range did this lab call HF?
questions.why: HF is 3 to 30 MHz. VHF and UHF are the higher ranges Lab 01 already labeled.

questions.stem: Why was the radio horizon farther than the visual horizon?
choices: The atmosphere bends VHF and UHF slightly
The radio wave is slower than light
Raising power extends the geometric horizon
questions.why: The classroom model uses a larger factor for the radio horizon than for the visual one. It is not a coverage prediction, and extra power does not move the geometric horizon.

questions.stem: A mobile signal flutters as the car moves a short distance and several reflections are arriving. What did the lab call that flutter?
questions.why: Multipath is several paths at once. The rapid mobile flutter is picket fencing. The same collisions can garble data.

questions.stem: Leaves are in a UHF path. What did the absorption model do with that energy?
choices: It absorbed much of it, so the signal got weaker
It turned the path into a reliable F-region hop
It had the same effect as fog on a 10-meter signal
questions.why: Vegetation absorbs UHF and microwave energy. Fog and rain barely affect 10-meter and 6-meter signals in this lab, and absorption is not the same as an ionospheric return.

questions.stem: The signal is a one-second burst on 6 meters during a meteor shower. Which path fits?
choices: A temperature inversion that lasts all afternoon
questions.why: Meteor trails scatter brief signals. Six meters is the band this lab associated with that path. A duct lasts longer, and a ridge does not need a meteor.

questions.stem: VHF stations a few hundred miles away are steady while a temperature inversion sits over the path. What is the fitting concept?
questions.why: An inversion can duct VHF and UHF well past the ordinary radio horizon. Aurora sounds raspy. Daytime absorption is an HF problem, not a VHF duct.

blocks.body: Propagation investigation. Each note has a place, a band, and what the operator heard. Pick the concept this lab taught. You are not forecasting tomorrow.

config.doneText: You matched each report to a path from this lab.

reports.text: A hiker on a ridge and a station in the valley are 20 miles apart on 2-meter FM. A hill sits between them. Raising the hiker's antenna clears the hill. The signal is steady.
reports.context: Band: 146 MHz. Time: afternoon. Terrain: one ridge.

choices.label: Line of sight, opened by antenna height
choices.why: This is the VHF path Lab 07 taught and this lab kept inside the radio horizon. Height cleared the obstacle.

choices.label: F-region skip
choices.why: Twenty miles of 2-meter FM with a ridge in the way is not an ionospheric hop.

reports.text: A 6-meter operator copies half-second bursts from a station they have never heard. A meteor shower is underway.
reports.context: Band: 50 MHz. Path: brief. No inversion reported.

choices.label: Meteor scatter
choices.why: The bursts and the band match meteor scatter.

choices.label: Picket fencing
choices.why: Picket fencing is rapid flutter while a vehicle moves through local reflections, not a distant burst.

reports.text: At noon, with high sunspot numbers, 10-meter SSB is coming in from another continent. The same band was quiet at the same hour last year when the sun was quiet.
reports.context: Band: 28 MHz. Time: day. Sunspots: high.

choices.label: F-region skip
choices.why: The lab's sketch opens long 10-meter paths in the daytime when sunspots are high.

choices.label: Rain absorption
choices.why: Rain is not what opens a worldwide 10-meter path, and this lab treats rain as a small effect on 10 meters.

reports.text: A VHF CW signal sounds like a rasp. Voice is almost unreadable. The aurora is visible to the north.
reports.context: Band: 144 MHz. Sound: distorted. Sky: aurora.

choices.label: Auroral propagation
choices.why: Scattering from the aurora makes the signal sound distorted. CW survives that better than voice in this lab.

choices.label: Knife-edge diffraction
choices.why: A ridge can weaken a signal. It does not rasp it because of an aurora.

blocks.body: Polarization matching is already in the course. These two conventions are additional.
